Mark Antony. A Roman military commander and political figure of the late Republic, most famous for his alliance with Julius Caesar, his role in the Second Triumvirate governing Rome after Caesar's death, and his romantic and political partnership with Cleopatra of Egypt. Ambitious and skilled in war, he ultimately was outmaneuvered by his rival Octavian, leading to his defeat and death in Egypt.

Mark Antony was born into a wealthy and political family with ties to the populist faction of the late Republic. He became an accomplished military officer and supporter of Julius Caesar, serving as his ally and subordinate during the Civil War against Pompey. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Antony positioned himself as Caesar's avenger and formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, Caesar's heir, and Marcus Lepidus, a general. The three men divided the Roman world into spheres and worked together against Caesar's assassins.

The Triumvirate engaged in proscriptions, killing political enemies, and civil war to consolidate power. Antony was particularly successful militarily against threats from Parthia in the east, though an invasion of Parthia itself proved costly and unsuccessful. Antony's alliance with Cleopatra of Egypt strengthened his position in the eastern Mediterranean. The two leaders combined resources, political legitimacy, and personal attraction to create a powerful eastern coalition against Octavian's growing power in the west.

The triumvirate gradually collapsed as Octavian maneuvered against his rivals, positioning himself as the defender of Rome against Antony and Cleopatra, whom he portrayed as under the spell of an exotic foreign queen. At the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra's naval forces in a decisive battle. Antony and Cleopatra retreated to Egypt, and when Octavian pursued them, Antony committed suicide rather than face capture.

Antony represented the old militaristic virtue of the Republic, while Octavian embodied the ruthlessness and political calculation that characterized imperial Rome. Antony's defeat marked the transition from the Republic to the Empire. He has been portrayed in literature and drama as a tragic figure, capable and charismatic but ultimately undone by his love for Cleopatra and by overambition, with Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra being the most famous literary treatment of his story.
